characterization_methods.key_findings: SROs about 2 nm in size were detected by weak superlattice reflections, randomly distributed in solution treated and water quenched Fe–28Mn–9Al–0.8C and Fe-30Mn-8Al-1.2C steels.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: solution treated and water quenched specimens
characterization_methods.purpose: to detect short-range ordering (weak superlattice reflections) and L'12 ordering in the austenite

characterization_methods.key_findings: The E moduli of Fe-(15–28)Mn-(7–10)Al-(0.7–1.2)C steels and of as-cast Fe-(5–40)Mn-10Al-1C steels were measured using the resonance method.
characterization_methods.purpose: to measure the Young's modulus of Fe-Mn-Al-C steels after different processing steps

characterization_methods.key_findings: The austenitic Fe-Mn-Al-C microstructure after hot rolling generally shows an equiaxed austenitic grain structure containing annealing twins.
characterization_methods.purpose: to characterise the microstructure of austenitic low density steels

computational_details.boundary_and_initial_conditions: graphite formation suppressed; isothermal sections at 900 °C and polythermal sections for Fe-Mn-Al-C compositions
computational_details.potential_model_or_database: FSstel database; Chin et al. Fe–Al–Mn–C description; Connétable et al. Fe–Al–C database
computational_details.simulation_method: CALPHAD thermodynamic calculation of phase equilibria
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: Calculations from different databases are similar but deviate from experimental phase boundaries, especially at high Mn and Al contents; calculated formation temperatures of α, (γ+κ) and M23C6 are systematically lower than measured.

analytical_models.equation_role: density of Fe-Mn-Al-C austenitic alloys as a function of composition (Eq. 2)
analytical_models.model_note: ρ_austenitic (g/cm3) = 8.15 − 0.101(wt%Al) − 0.41(wt%C) − 0.0085(wt%Mn); 1.3% density reduction per 1 wt% Al addition.

analytical_models.equation_role: composition boundary for precipitation of the intragranular κ0 phase in Fe-Mn-Al-C alloys (Eq. 3)
analytical_models.model_name: Huang composition boundary for intragranular κ0 precipitation
analytical_models.model_note: 0.098(wt%Al) + 0.208(wt%C) = 1 − 0.0054(wt%Mn); intragranular κ0 precipitates only when Al > 7% and C > 0.7%.

defect_interactions.interaction_type: dislocation–SRO/κ'-carbide interaction (glide plane softening, shearing of κ'-carbides)
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: The initial dislocation moving through the FCC lattice destroys the SRO and faces higher resistance than following dislocations, localising plastic deformation into slip bands (glide plane softening); in highly alloyed/aged steels cuboidal κ'-carbides are sheared by dislocations, enhancing planar slip.

interfaces.interface_notes: In the γ (FCC) phase the lattice parameter of the κ phase is 0.383–0.386 nm and γ/κ interfaces are coherent (lattice mismatch < 3%), whereas in the α (BCC) phase the κ lattice parameter is 0.387–0.389 nm and α/κ interfaces are semicoherent (mismatch 6%).
interfaces.phase_evolution: γ → γ' + γ'' → γ' + L12 (SRO) → γ' + κ' (spinodal decomposition followed by an ordering reaction); the L12 phase transforms to the E21 κ'-carbide by further ordering of carbon atoms.

phase_interfaces.coherence: coherent (lattice misfit < 3%); cube-on-cube orientation relationship [100]κ//[100]γ and [010]κ//[010]γ

interfaces.slip_behavior: Planar glide dominates the plastic deformation of austenitic Fe-Mn-Al-C steels regardless of SFE and aging conditions; no dislocation cell formation is observed.

comparative_performance.comparison_metric: CVN impact energy at room temperature

comparative_performance.benchmark_alloy_id: Mn TWIP steel and conventional deep drawing steels (DC04, HC300LA, IF)
comparative_performance.improvement_percentage: ~50% higher than conventional deep drawing steels (0.16–0.25 J/mm3)

comparative_performance.benchmark_alloy_id: austenitic Cr-Ni steel and martensitic Cr steel

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Solution treatment is carried out in the single austenite (γ) phase area. For the reviewed tensile series the steels were solutionized at 1100 °C for 2 h (Fig. 27) or at 1000 °C/1 h (Fig. 22a). Cold rolled strips of age-hardenable austenitic Fe-Mn-Al-C steels are solution treated in this range prior to quenching.

Fast cooling (water quenching) from the solution treatment temperature to room temperature to avoid formation of coarse intergranular κ-carbide and/or α-particles. Quenching may be in water, oil or other quench media.

chemical.corrosion_resistance: far inferior to 304 stainless steel; comparable to conventional high strength steels

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: solution treated and water quenched condition; tensile direction parallel to strip rolling direction
measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: tensile specimens; geometry normalised to ASTM E-8 (gauge length 50 mm, width 12.5 mm, thickness 1 mm) for the TE comparison of Fig. 25
measurement_conditions.test_standard: ASTM E-8 (for the TE conversion used in Fig. 25)

strain_hardening_rate.value: Strain hardening is dominated by planar glide/planar slip; strain hardening rate of Al-containing austenitic steels is always lower than that of Al-free Mn TWIP steel, and highly alloyed or peak-aged ST+WQ steels can show near-horizontal or negative work hardening.

fracture_toughness.value: 200 J/cm2 (CVN impact energy at room temperature); dynamic fracture toughness 71.5 J/cm2 in the solution-treated condition

aliases: solution treated and water quenched condition

phases_present.morphology: equiaxed polygonal grains containing annealing twins
coherent nano-sized particles / short-range ordered zones

precipitates.coherency: coherent with the austenite matrix (lattice misfit < 3%)
precipitates.distribution: randomly distributed / homogeneous within the austenite matrix

structures.overall_structure: Single-phase austenite (γ) with short-range orders (SROs) or uniformly distributed nano-sized κ'-carbides in the matrix, the decomposition products of austenite depending on the Al and C contents and on the cooling rate after solution treatment. Alloys with high Al and C form κ' directly during water quenching; alloys with lower Al develop only SRO.

unmapped_findings: Water quenching of austenitic Fe-Mn-Al-C steels can produce a single austenite phase with SROs that exhibits a high tensile strength and high ductility (b0255).

Fast cooling (water quenching) from solution treatment is used to avoid formation of coarse intergranular κ-carbide and/or α-particles; slow cooling or coiling produces κ-carbides about 3–6 times larger than those obtained after solutionizing, quenching and aging at around 550 °C, decreasing ductility and toughness (b0118).

The effective Al composition window for the best combination of mechanical properties in austenitic Fe-Mn-Al-C steels is narrow (between 7 and 10% Al); typical compositions are 15–30% Mn, 7–10% Al and 0.7–1.2% C with balance Fe (b0305).

The strength decreases but elongation increases as the solution temperature is increased (due to a larger austenite grain size); the strength increases as the cooling rate after solution treatment is decreased, due to the formation of a higher density of SRO or κ0-precipitates (b0239).
For Fe-30Mn-1.2C-xAl steels in the range 0–9% Al the microstructure after solution treatment is a single-phase austenite; δ-ferrite is introduced when the Al content exceeds 10% (b0230).
In alloys containing high Al (>7%) and C (>1.0%), metastable κ-carbides (L'12) may form during quenching after solution treatment, increasing strength without impairing elongation (b0230).
The addition of 2.5% Al to an Fe-18Mn-0.6C alloy suppresses deformation-induced twinning in the solution heat-treated and water quenched condition (b0182).
